observations.text: Understanding the genetic architecture of schizophrenia (SCZ) is invaluable for the development of personalized treatment. In three independent cohorts, using an automated pipeline, we calculated 413 psychiatry-relevant polygenic scores. Using these scores, machine learning was applied to stratify SCZ patients into two genetic risk profiles (GRP) in FinnGen (nSCZ=7 486), and to validate these results in the PsyCourse Study (nSCZ=419) and Bari (nSCZ=531). This illustrates that the penetrance of genetic SCZ risk might partially depend on the predisposition for the aforementioned traits through pleiotropic variants. metadata.summary: Background. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is associated with mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress. Our goal was to determine the effects of the dual SGLT1 and SGLT2 inhibitor sotagliflozin (SOTA) on myocardial remodeling, diastolic function, mitochondrial gene expression and oxidative stress in mice with HCM due to the tropomyosin E180G mutation (E180G). At 8 weeks mice were sacrificed to assess myocardial histology, RNA expression, oxidative stress and oxidative sulfonylation of sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPase (SERCA). Results. At baseline E180G mice had myocardial hypertrophy, interstitial fibrosis, diastolic dysfunction and atrial enlargement - all of which worsened over the next 8 weeks. In E180G mice treatment with SOTA for 8 weeks prevented further LV hypertrophy and atrial enlargement, decreased interstitial fibrosis and normalized diastolic function. Mitochondrial gene sets were downregulated, and oxidative stress was increased and associated with oxidative sulfonylation of SERCA at C674. SOTA treatment upregulated mitochondrial gene sets and prevented the increases in oxidative stress and SERCA oxidation. Upregulated fibrosis gene sets in E180G hearts were not affected by SOTA. In E180G hearts, SOTA corrected the HCM phenotype, normalized diastolic function, upregulated mitochondrial gene sets, and decreased oxidative stress and SERCA oxidation. observations.text: Single cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) has revolutionized cellular biology over the past decade. At its most basic, a scRNAseq dataset is a cell by gene matrix with entries giving the transcription count of a particular gene in a particular cell. A common workflow applies log-normalization and z-scoring to the count matrix and then embeds the cells in a lower dimensional space using principal component analysis (PCA). A large number of computational tools use the PCA embedding as a starting point, but statistical models for the distribution of cells in the PCA space are lacking. As a result, many tools depend on ad-hoc assumptions that likely lead to signal loss. In this work, we address this gap using the metacell model, a statistical model of count matrices introduced by previous authors. We show that application of the workflow to count matrices generated under a metacell model yields PCA embeddings distributed as a Gaussian mixture model (GMM). To our knowledge, this is the first result connecting a statistical model of counts to the distribution of cells in PCA space. Our derivation depends on methods from random matrix theory (RMT) and we extend and establish connections between RMT and scRNAseq count matrices. We then use the predicted GMM to test the metacell model on 11 datasets. The predictions are accurate for counts generated by the metacell model but underestimate the variance of real cells for most of our datasets. We show that this error largely arises from gene correlations within metacells, which the metacell model does not capture. Some of our datasets are fit relatively well by the metacell model, suggesting that the fit of the metacell model to true datasets depends on sufficiently dense sampling. Finally, we show that the strength of noise in the PCA space varies significantly across metacells, suggesting that statistical modeling of PCA embeddings can improve existing downstream workflows. Our results provide a framework for deriving and testing statistical models of PCA embeddings from statistical models of counts and identify a limitation of the metacell description for scRNAseq datasets.

BackgroundLarge language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to support systematic review and meta-analysis, but complex evidence flow, trial-family identification, study-level data extraction, and statistical execution remain vulnerable to omissions, untraceable data paths, and scientifically flawed steps. It remains unclear whether gains are driven by modular skills or by fixed orchestration, and whether these effects differ across base models.

MethodsWe conducted a controlled, multi-model benchmark in which six LLMs completed the same randomized controlled trial (RCT) meta-analysis task under three conditions: (A) no meta-analysis-specific skills; (B) autonomous access to modular meta-analysis skills; and (C) the same skills executed under a Quality-First fixed directed acyclic graph (DAG). Each model was run three times per condition (54 runs total). The primary outcome was the scientific performance score (SPS, 0-100), rated by two meta-analysis experts; one expert was masked to explicit model and condition labels during SPS scoring, and final scores were the arithmetic mean of the two raters. Inter-rater reliability was high (SPS ICC(A,2) = 0.991).

ResultsMean SPS was 43.50 (condition A), 55.65 (B), and 54.44 (C). Relative to unassisted models, modular skills improved mean SPS by +12.15 points (unadjusted 95% CI 3.15-21.16; Holm-adjusted P = 0.033). The combined modular-skills-plus-fixed-DAG condition showed a positive but not statistically significant difference relative to unassisted models (C - A = +10.94; Holm-adjusted P = 0.073) and no incremental gain over skills alone (C - B = - 1.21; Holm-adjusted P = 0.746). No condition-by-model interaction was detected (P = 0.801).

ConclusionsIn this benchmark task, access to modular skills improved mean scientific performance relative to unassisted execution; fixed orchestration of the same skills did not provide a detectable incremental benefit. The findings are task-specific and do not establish general effects for other meta-analysis settings, models, or orchestration designs.

metadata.summary: Epidermal growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EGFR-TKIs) exhibit limited efficacy against lung cancer brain metastases, often resulting in rapid and inevitable resistance. However, the unique mechanisms driving this brain microenvironment-specific therapeutic failure remain elusive. Here, utilizing in vivo orthotopic models and single-cell RNA sequencing, we reveal that targeted therapy induces a distinct, metabolically hyperactive senescent cell subpopulation that drives rapid EGFR-TKI tolerance in brain metastasis. We identify the molecular chaperone CRYAB as an indispensable driver specifically upregulated within this senescent persister state. Mechanistically, CRYAB physically interacts with VDAC2 at the outer mitochondrial membrane, promoting endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-mitochondria tethering and calcium influx. This CRYAB-VDAC2 axis orchestrates adaptive mitochondrial fission, hyperactivating oxidative metabolism while simultaneously shielding（preventing？） senescent cells from fatal oxidative stress. Genetic or pharmacological blockade of mitochondrial fission completely abolishes CRYAB-mediated therapeutic resistance. Therapeutically, we demonstrate that a 25-hydroxycholesterol (25HC) dietary intervention acts as a potent in vivo senolytic strategy, directly dismantling the CRYAB-dependent resistance network, eradicating senescent persister cells, and synergistically prolonging overall survival when combined with Osi. Furthermore, high baseline CRYAB expression in pre-treatment primary lung biopsies clinically predicts lower intracranial objective response rates and shorter progression-free survival in a cohort of advanced EGFR-mutant NSCLC patients. Collectively, our study uncovers a novel CRYAB-VDAC2-mitochondrial fission axis that enforces therapy-induced senescence and highlights 25HC dietary intervention as a highly translatable combinatorial strategy to overcome EGFR-TKI resistance in brain metastasis.

observations.text: Marker-based optical motion capture remains the gold standard for kinematic analysis across biomechanical research. However, when tracking dynamic movements, severe occlusions often create missing data and noisy signals that require time-consuming manual cleaning. Existing automated methods usually rely on predefined skeleton models or need massive training datasets for machine learning solutions. This study presents the AMP: an automated marker based motion capture processing pipeline. The AMP is a fully analytical approach that uses hierarchical algorithms including 1) rigid-body constraint, 2) Kalman Filter state estimation and 3) kinematic pattern match to label markers and fill data gaps without manual human intervention. First, the algorithm identifies and removes mislabeling markers before any data scrubbing. During the data cleaning process, our hierarchical algorithm uses a translation-based step to track segments even when there are insufficient donor markers to form a full rigid body. To reconstruct missing marker trajectories, the pipeline initially uses Piecewise Cubic Hermite Interpolating Polynomial (PCHIP) interpolation for short marker gaps. However, the PCHIP creates massive spatial errors during long occlusions, the system automatically switches to rigid-body tracking for gaps over 40 ms. Results showed the pipeline drastically reduced processing time compared to manual human expert methods by 73.5%. In addition, the AMP kept spatial errors within 10 mm of the manual ground truth. By using this combined hierarchical approach to match marker processing accuracy, the pipeline provides a fast, general-purpose tool that fully automates data cleaning and saves hours of manual effort.
observations.title: AMP: An Automated Marker Based Motion Capture Processing Pipeline for Kinematic Trajectory Label Scrubbing and Gaps Filling

observations.text: Infectious disease forecasting supports public health preparedness and response by informing resource allocation, intervention planning, and situational awareness. Infectious disease forecasting capabilities in the United States have grown over the past decade yet whether forecast quality has improved over this time remains unclear. Current evaluation metrics describe relative performance for a common set of forecast targets but cannot evaluate performance across different outcomes, seasons, and pathogens. We addressed this challenge by developing a novel skill score metric to assess forecasts based on performance relative to two benchmark models: a hindcast as an idealized upper bound of performance and a baseline model as a minimal performance standard. To study the impact of the baseline choice, we considered three types of baseline models with varying levels of complexity. Using this skill score framework, we retrospectively evaluated short-term influenza (influenza-like illness and hospitalization) and COVID-19 (case, death, and hospitalization) forecasts, focusing on how the performance of team and multi-model ensemble forecasts changed over time. The ensemble outperformed 99% of forecasts from a simplistic, naive baseline, and 84-91% of forecasts from more complex baseline models that incorporate recent data. We found consistent improvements in ensemble and team forecast skill over time for both influenza forecast targets, with 4-week horizon forecasts in the most recent year having higher skill scores than 1-week horizon forecasts in the first year of each challenge. Results were mixed for COVID-19 forecasts. This framework provides a comprehensive picture of progress in infectious disease forecasting over the past decade enabled by improved standardization, data, models, and collaboration.
observations.title: Quantifying advances in infectious disease forecast skill across seasons and pathogens

metadata.summary: Aims: Sinoatrial node (SAN) dysfunction is commonly observed in obesity and diabetes and is associated with increased cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. Cardiac steatosis, characterized by excessive intracellular lipid droplet (LD) accumulation in cardiomyocytes, is common in these metabolic disorders, but its direct contribution to SAN dysfunction remains unclear. We investigated whether intracellular LD accumulation impairs SAN automaticity. Methods and Results: Transgenic mice (TG) with cardiomyocyte-specific overexpression of perilipin 2 (PLIN2) and double-transgenic mice (DTG) co-expressing PLIN2 and hormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) were studied. TG mice exhibited marked LD accumulation in SAN myocytes together with prolonged and highly variable R–R intervals on electrocardiography (ECG). Optical Ca²⁺ mapping of SAN–atrial preparations demonstrated displacement of the leading pacemaker site toward peripheral nodal and extranodal regions in TG mice. Isolated TG SAN myocytes exhibited reduced sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca²⁺ content, attenuated local Ca²⁺ releases (LCRs), and elevated intracellular and mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels. In contrast, mitochondrial and SR ultrastructure were unaltered, and global gene expression profiles were preserved, except for PLIN2 overexpression. Normalization of intracellular LD accumulation by HSL co-expression prevented abnormalities in ECG, SAN automaticity, intracellular Ca²⁺ handling, and ROS levels despite persistent PLIN2 overexpression. This study was limited by the use of male mice, and the causal contribution of elevated ROS to the observed SAN dysfunction was not directly tested. Conclusion: Intracellular LD accumulation alone was sufficient to alter intracellular Ca²⁺ handling and impair SAN automaticity. Normalization of intracellular LD accumulation by HSL co-expression prevented SAN dysfunction, supporting a causal role for intracellular LD accumulation in pacemaker dysfunction. These findings identify myocardial steatosis as a previously underrecognized contributor to SAN dysfunction.

observations.title: Excess accumulation of intracellular lipid droplet impairs sinoatrial function in a mouse model of myocardial steatosis

metadata.summary: Nutraceuticals such as (+)-Catechin are emerging as promising agents for the prevention and treatment of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. A large prospective study of 34,492 participants previously demonstrated an inverse association between (+)-Catechin intake and risk for coronary heart disease. Our recent work further showed that (+)-Catechin inhibits several atherosclerosis related processes in vitro, induces beneficial metabolic changes in male C57BL/6J mice fed a high fat diet (HFD), and reduces plaque burden and inflammation in male low-density lipoprotein (LDL) receptor deficient (LDLr / ) mice fed a HFD. Given known sex specific differences in atherosclerosis, it is essential to extend these investigations to female mice. The objective of this study was therefore to investigate the effects of (+)-Catechin in female LDLr /  mice in vivo. (+)-Catechin lowered plasma cholesterol levels, reduced circulating T cell populations, and increased several beneficial short chain fatty acids in both the plasma and the faeces. It also decreased plaque size, lipid content, macrophage accumulation, and CD3⁺ T cell infiltration in the aortic root, while enhancing markers of plaque stability. RNA sequencing (RNA seq) of the thoracic aorta revealed modulation of key pathways involved in inflammatory signalling, hypertension and immune responses. Complementary studies in human aortic smooth muscle cells demonstrated that (+)-Catechin attenuated macropinocytosis and oxidised LDL uptake, processes linked to plaque progression, without promoting calcification. RNA seq identified several genes and pathways consistent with the compound’s anti atherogenic and plaque stabilising actions. Collectively, these findings provide new mechanistic insights into the beneficial cardiovascular effects of (+)-Catechin in female mice and support further evaluation of this flavanol in human clinical trials.

Single-nucleus RNA-seq revealed that endothelial matrin-3 deficiency impairs signaling and promotes inflammation in hepatocytes. Finally, matrin-3 expression was reduced in mouse and human atherosclerotic plaques. These results demonstrate that endothelial matrin-3 limits cellular senescence, which maintains lipid homeostasis via paracrine effects; its expression in the vascular endothelium protects mice from the development of atherosclerosis.

observations.text: Climate change is increasingly disrupting the relationship between locally adapted populations and the environments in which they evolved, creating an urgent need for tools that connect genomic variation to climate. Common-garden and provenance trials remain the gold standard for characterizing local adaptation, but their time and resource requirements limit how broadly they can be applied. Genomic approaches provide a complementary path. Genotype--environment association (GEA) methods identify environmentally associated loci. Machine-learning models have also shown that geographic origin can be predicted directly from genotypes. Here we introduce EcoLocator, a supervised deep neural network that jointly predicts geographic location and climate of origin from genotypes. Through extensive simulations we demonstrate that EcoLocator accurately recovers geographic location and environment of origin from genotype data, and, with SHAP-based feature attribution, identifies adaptive loci more reliably than benchmark GEA methods. We apply our method to coastal Douglas-fir (Pseudotsuga menziesii var. menziesii), where EcoLocator predicts geographic origin (R2=0.75--0.83) and climate of origin (R2=0.52--0.72) under leave-one-out cross-validation. Notably, we find that climate predicted directly from genotypes outperforms climate inferred by first predicting geographic origin, showing that EcoLocator captures genotype--climate signal that cannot be recovered from geography alone. Our prediction errors fall within the tolerances used in existing seed-transfer guidelines, demonstrating that EcoLocator's predictions are ready for practical application, and our approach is readily extendable to other species and conservation contexts.

observations.text: During biogeographical ancestry (BGA) analysis, an unknown individual for whom ancestry informative markers (AIMs) were analyzed is often assigned to one of a few reference populations. For some individuals, such an assignment is not meaningful: the two parents of the individual may come from different populations, or the individual may come from a population not included in the reference database. In this study, we examined classification methods in combination with 104 AIMs from the VISAGE Enhanced Tool to provide one of the following three possible outcomes: (i) in-reference (IR), with an assignment to one of the reference populations; (ii) admixed (AD), with parents from two in-reference populations; and (iii) out-of-reference (OR), where the individual's ancestry is not sufficiently represented by the reference populations. We therefore compared seven classifiers in combination with class-specific acceptance thresholds for the OR decision. The best-performing method according to our selection criterion was a naive Bayes classifier over pairs of populations, which we call the recent naive Bayes (RNB) classifier. Populations held out of the reference panel were correctly rejected in $84.9\%$ of cases. We further tested the method on $800$ individuals from seven additional groups not included in the reference panel. Only $29.4\%$ of individuals from four non-admixed populations were rejected, resembling joint ancestry with reference populations. In addition, we investigated the prediction accuracy in a newly collected dataset of 28 individuals with self-reported ancestry by analyzing AIMs using massively parallel sequencing.
observations.title: In which cases does it make sense to classify an individual into one population and what are the alternatives?

metadata.summary: The myocardium contains three resident macrophage subsets with distinct gene expression and functions in cardiac injury and disease. However, the underlying epigenetic structure of resident cardiac macrophages and the epigenetic signature of each individual subset is poorly understood. Here, we used single-cell and bulk ATAC sequencing to generate a chromatin accessibility landscape of macrophages from the healthy murine myocardium. Bulk sequencing of each subset revealed 2 chromatin accessibility signatures that corresponded with either resident CCR2+ macrophages, or resident CCR2- macrophages that diverged transcriptionally to give rise to TLF+ (TIMD4+LYVE1+FOLR2+) or MHC-IIhi (TLF-) subsets. Footprint analysis demonstrated subset-specific differences in transcription factor binding – particularly, enrichment of AP-1 in CCR2+ macrophages, and increased MAF binding in TLF+ macrophages. Furthermore, we demonstrate that loss of MAF factor MAFB in myeloid cells disrupts TLF+ macrophage-specific gene expression and skews subset composition toward CCR2+ MFs. Finally, we identify a link between the transcription factor IRF8 and MHC-II, in which loss of IRF8 abolished MHC-II expression exclusively in CCR2- subsets but not CCR2+ macrophages. This granular characterization of the epigenetic and transcriptional substructure of cardiac macrophages

observations.text:
Background/AimsThis work aimed to estimate the annual tertiary healthcare and societal costs associated with paediatric congenital heart disease (CHD) in the United Kingdom using real-world data from a Level 1 cardiac surgical centre in the National Health Service (NHS).

MethodsA prevalence-based cost-of-illness analysis was conducted using patient-level inpatient and outpatient activity data from Evelina London Childrens Hospital between 1 June 2023 and 31 May 2024. Costs were estimated from NHS and societal perspectives and extrapolated to national level using National Congenital Heart Disease Audit (NCHDA) procedural activity data. Healthcare costs included tertiary centre care costs. Societal costs included parental productivity losses and impacts on lifetime earnings for children. Deterministic sensitivity analysis explored parameter uncertainty.

ResultsApproximately 9.6% of UK paediatric CHD procedures were undertaken at Evelina London Childrens Hospital at a cost of {pound}15.0 million per annum, corresponding to a national estimate of {pound}156.4 million. Single-ventricle procedures accounted for 4.8% of inpatient activity but 19.4% of inpatient costs. Sensitivity analysis produced national healthcare cost estimates ranging from {pound}125.1 million to {pound}187.7 million.

National productivity losses associated with parental absence from work were estimated at {pound}82.4 million annually. Individuals with CHD were estimated to experience a mean reduction in lifetime earnings of {pound}81,509.

ConclusionPaediatric CHD imposes a substantial economic cost on the UK healthcare system and wider society. This study provides the first real-world national estimate of the economic impact of paediatric CHD in the UK and may inform future service planning, research investment, and innovation adoption strategies.

Key Learning points1. What is already known

* Congenital heart disease (CHD) is the most common congenital abnormality worldwide and requires substantial healthcare utilisation throughout childhood, including outpatient monitoring, hospital admissions, surgical and catheter interventions.

* Existing evidence suggests that CHD is associated with high healthcare costs and wider societal impacts; however, available economic burden studies have been conducted in the United States and are not generalisable to the UK healthcare system.

* The broader economic consequences of paediatric CHD, including parental productivity losses and impacts on future employment and earnings, remain poorly quantified in the UK.

2. What this study adds

* This study provides, to our knowledge, the first UK-wide estimate of the economic burden of paediatric CHD using real-world patient-level activity and cost data from a large volume tertiary centre.

* Annual direct NHS costs associated with paediatric CHD care at tertiary settings were estimated at {pound}156.4 million nationally, with an additional {pound}82.4 million in parental productivity losses, demonstrating a substantial societal burden beyond healthcare expenditure alone.

* Infants and patients with severe CHD requiring single-ventricle procedures accounted for a disproportionately large share of costs, highlighting important targets for future service improvement, research investment, and innovation.

metadata.summary: The prevalence of neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) is increasing, with growing evidence implicating the intrauterine environment as a critical regulator of fetal brain development. Gestational perturbations such as maternal stress can increase NDD risk; however, the mechanism(s) by which prenatal maternal stress reshape fetal neurodevelopment remain unclear. Accordingly, the objective of my project was to characterize how maternal cold stress exposure during pregnancy disrupts neural stem and progenitor cell (NSPC) developmental programs in the fetus and the impact this has on neurodevelopment in the hypothalamus. Pregnant mice were exposed to 4°C for 30 minutes daily from embryonic day 11.5 (E11.5) to E15.5—a critical period of neurodevelopment in the hypothalamus. To assess how maternal cold stress impacts neural stem cell (NSC) behaviours, we employed the neurosphere assay, quantifying the number and size of primary and secondary neurospheres as a measure of NSC proliferation and self-renewal, respectively. Our findings revealed no change in NSC proliferation or self-renewal when comparing control and maternal cold stress male and female neurospheres. However, differentiation of dissociated NSCs revealed that neurons from both sexes had longer axons following maternal cold stress exposure. Interestingly, only male-derived cultures exhibited a significant increase in the number TUJ1+ neurons in response to maternal cold stress exposure, whereas only female-derived maternal cold stress cultures showed enhanced dendritic arborization. To explore the molecular basis of these changes, we performed single-cell RNA sequencing on E15.5 fetal hypothalamic NSPCs. Analysis of differentially expressed genes uncovered basal sex differences between the transcriptional signatures of control male and female Cycling NSPCs and suggested that maternal cold stress shifts female Cycling NSPCs toward a more male-like transcriptional profile. Gene ontology analysis revealed that maternal cold stress upregulates pathways linked to neuronal growth, development, and GABAergic neuron differentiation, but only in females. Importantly, ligand-receptor analysis suggested that maternal cold stress exposure disrupts neurodevelopmental programs through altered cell-cell signalling within Cycling NSPCs predominantly in females. These findings demonstrate that prenatal maternal cold stress exposure drives sex-specific effects on fetal neurodevelopment and uncover distinct cellular pathways that may contribute to sex differences seen in the presentation and risk of many NDDs.

observations.title: Prenatal maternal cold stress exposure drives sex-specific neurodevelopmental disruptions in the fetal hypothalamus

observations.text: During sleep and quiet wakefulness, the brain spontaneously revisits neural activity patterns associated with previous experience, a phenomenon known as reactivation, or replay. Reactivation is thought to support systems consolidation, the process by which memory retrieval becomes progressively more dependent on neocortical circuits and less dependent on the hippocampus. Importantly, reactivation is not indiscriminate: some memory traces, such as newly acquired or weakly learned ones, are preferentially reactivated. These observations have motivated the development of computational models accounting for the spontaneous reactivation of memory traces, their prioritisation for replay, and their transfer between the hippocampus and neocortex. In parallel, predictive-coding (PC) models have shown how computations attributed to hippocampal and neocortical circuits can arise from local prediction-error dynamics. Here, we connect these two lines of work by showing how autonomous intrinsic dynamics in coupled PC networks can transfer stored memory content between neural systems. The hippocampus and neocortex are modelled as two coupled PC associative memory networks, with asymmetric coupling motivated by reported interactions between hippocampal area CA1 and the prefrontal cortex. This coupling establishes a closed-loop hippocampal-neocortical dialogue in which hippocampal activity drives neocortical learning, while neocortical feedback biases subsequent hippocampal activity toward content for which neocortical support remains weak. We prove that this feedback steers hippocampal activity toward states of higher neocortical free energy, so that prioritisation emerges from the dialogue itself rather than from an explicit scheduler. In our model, neocortical learning relies exclusively on spontaneous hippocampal activity, without access to the initial training corpus. Nevertheless, we show that the neocortical network acquires correlated memory content faster than direct training on randomly sampled memory patterns. This advantage appeared for sufficiently correlated patterns, grew with their correlation, and persisted when new patterns were incrementally added during transfer. Together, these results provide a PC account in which neocortical feedback organises hippocampal reactivation to support efficient transfer of memory content during systems consolidation.
observations.title: Selective Hippocampal Reactivation Driven by Neocortical Feedback Supports Memory Transfer in Predictive-Coding Networks

BackgroundThe National Early Warning Score (NEWS) is widely used to predict patient deterioration, but retrospective validations face intervention bias and emphasise discrimination over clinical utility. We aimed to compare NEWSs clinical net benefit against simplified scoring rules and machine learning, to determine whether simpler approaches suffice or if complex models offer meaningful advantages, and to evaluate performance heterogeneity across patient subgroups.

MethodsWe included fifteen Danish hospitals with over 2{middle dot}08 million hospital encounters representing 825200 unique patients over five years (2018 to 2023). We compared NEWS against both simpler and more complex approaches for predicting 24h mortality: Simplified NEWS (NEWS without blood pressure and temperature), DEWS (Simplified NEWS with age and sex), and a model based on eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGB-EWS) incorporating vital signs, demographics, laboratory markers, plus medical history embeddings extracted using sentence transformers. We used propensity score weighting to mitigate intervention bias and evaluated performance using net benefit, Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUC), and calibration.

FindingsDecision curve analysis in the overall population showed maximum net benefit differences of 1{middle dot}9 additional correct mortality identifications per 10000 patients between XGB-EWS and NEWS, and 1{middle dot}5 per 10000 between NEWS and Simplified NEWS. However, stratified analyses revealed substantial heterogeneity: in the high-risk group (initial NEWS [≥]7), XGB-EWS provided a maximum gain of 78{middle dot}1 correct identifications per 10000 patients compared to NEWS, while Simplified NEWS resulted in a maximum performance loss of 60{middle dot}2 per 10000. Conversely, in low-risk groups, differences were minimal.

InterpretationModel complexity produced limited average clinical utility gains, concentrated among patients initially classified as high risk by NEWS. These findings support prospective trials of risk-stratified monitoring based on the first NEWS assessment, testing simplified approaches for lower-risk patients while retaining full NEWS or electronic health-record models for higher-risk patients.

FundingNovo Nordisk Foundation

Research in context

Evidence before this studyEarly warning score systems have evolved from single vital sign monitoring to standardized multivariable scores such as the National Early Warning Score (NEWS), to even more sophisticated machine learning and deep learning frameworks utilizing electronic health records data. All these early warning scores are primarily designed to guide clinical decision-making by helping identify patients at risk of clinical deterioration within hospitals. Despite these advances, validation studies predominantly focus on statistical metrics measuring discrimination performance rather than meaningful clinical utility. On May 23, 2026 we searched PubMed for studies without language limitations published from May 23, 2016, to May 23, 2026, using terms including "early warning score", "NEWS", "NEWS2", "machine learning", "artificial intelligence", "decision curve analysis", "net benefit", "clinical utility", and "24-hour mortality." While most of the published models, including the more sophisticated machine learning ones, have demonstrated better discrimination compared to traditional early warning scores, we found only one study that combined early warning score validation with clinical utility analysis for short-term clinical deterioration. Additionally, no studies have evaluated clinical utility across multiple patient subgroups while using causal inference approaches to address intervention bias in a large-scale healthcare system validation.

Added value of this studyThe current work is a large-scale multi-center early warning score validation study, encompassing 2{middle dot}08 million hospital encounters across 15 Danish hospitals and nine distinct clinical specialties over five years. We used the predictimand framework with causal inference methods to address intervention bias, a critical methodological advance in early warning score assessment. Unlike previous research focused primarily on discrimination metrics, we evaluated clinical utility using decision curve analysis across multiple patient subgroups, revealing heterogeneity in net benefit differences. In the overall population, sophisticated machine learning approaches provided marginal improvements (up to 1{middle dot}9 per 10000 patients) despite superior discrimination, and simplified NEWS (without blood pressure and temperature) achieved comparable net benefit to full NEWS. However, in high-risk subgroups, particularly patients with high initial NEWS scores, differences increased substantially (up to 78{middle dot}1 per 10000 for machine learning versus NEWS and 60{middle dot}2 per 10000 for NEWS versus simplified NEWS), indicating that implementation strategies should be tailored to clinical context rather than uniformly applied.

Implications of all the available evidenceWe demonstrated that differences in mortality prediction varied substantially by baseline risk: less than 2 per 10000 patients in the overall population, but up to 78 per 10000 in high-risk subgroups such as patients with initial high scores of NEWS. These findings challenge uniform implementation approaches: for general ward screening where most patients are at low baseline risk, simplified scoring achieves comparable utility while potentially enabling workflow optimization. However, for high-risk populations where baseline mortality is elevated, more complex models provide larger incremental gains that may justify additional implementation complexity. Future research should conduct prospective cluster-randomized trials evaluating context-specific implementation strategies, comparing simplified versus complex approaches across different care settings and baseline risk profiles.
observations.title: Development and validation of early warning scores predicting 24-hour mortality addressing intercurrent medical interventions: a multi-centre retrospective cohort study of 2,08 million hospital encounters

The uptake of new digital and AI based technologies in the healthcare setting, including digital diagnostics, has been comparatively slower than in other sectors. This is a consequence of the complex legislature, and the lack of routine procedures for the secondary use of sensitive medical data. Inadequate level of education and incentives for different stakeholders prevents overcoming strong barriers, such as clinical workflow integration, and need for comprehensive evaluation of utility of interventions which requires multi-disciplinary collaboration effort. The paper presents a re-hospitalization challenge, organised by the European digital innovation hub (EDIH) - AI4Health.Cro, a co-creation activity and an effective tool for overcoming the mentioned barriers for implementation of new AI technologies and overall innovation ecosystem maturation. Crowdsourcing challenges or datathons are R&D strategies where ad-hoc assembled competing teams collaborate on early-stage technology development or research problem solving. Our re-hospitalisation challenge has had multiple facets: as activity for construction of an AI predictive model with explanatory support and plausible business model for its deployment; it involved also extensive organisers effort: data anonymisation, provision of secure processing environment, and comprehensive assessment of solutions. The paper details the challenge structure and processes, from problem inception to execution and evaluation. As a co-creation effort in digital healthcare, the challenge provided results on multiple levels: (i) tailored solutions based on primary data, serving as prototypes for later deployment in practice; (ii) sandboxing EHDS principles to enable secondary data use; (iii) ecosystem building event yielding cross-disciplinary participative learning experience. Innovation challenges arent just competitions; they are a building tool that provides several direct and indirect impacts, from developing healthcare technologies, supporting startups, to streamlining secondary use of clinical data for research and innovation and eliciting regulatory needs. Raising the awareness of all relevant stakeholders about the translation of AI technologies into routine clinical setting.

This slow progress largely reflects the complexity of EU legislation and the lack of practical procedures that translate legal requirements into guidance for stakeholders using sensitive medical data in research and innovation. A crowdsourcing pilot to predict likelihood of early rehospitalisation using AI methodology provided opportunity for hands-on experience for experts from clinical, computational and business background on both synthetic and real-world medical data. Together we clarify legal responsibilities and data access conditions, and facilitate collaboration of relevant stakeholders, clinical, technical, public and research entities for ecosystem building. We provide the first Croatian European Health Data Space compliant secure processing environment, created for future use by researchers and innovators. Methodologically varied AI based prototypes were developed to predict early rehospitalization carefully balancing data overfitting, AI explainability and market potential of technology, in turn raising multidisciplinary skills, and awareness of conditions required for innovation to thrive in 28 participating teams. This type of competition, provided within European Digital Innovation Hub is an ideal platform to build regulatory sandboxes and pilot novel legislative platforms ahead of their full-scale implementation.

metadata.summary: Nutraceuticals such as (+)-Catechin are emerging as promising agents for the prevention and treatment of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. A large prospective study of 34,492 participants previously demonstrated an inverse association between (+)-Catechin intake and risk for coronary heart disease. Our recent work further showed that (+)-Catechin inhibits several atherosclerosis related processes in vitro, induces beneficial metabolic changes in male C57BL/6J mice fed a high fat diet (HFD), and reduces plaque burden and inflammation in male low-density lipoprotein (LDL) receptor deficient (LDLr / ) mice fed a HFD. Given known sex specific differences in atherosclerosis, it is essential to extend these investigations to female mice. The objective of this study was therefore to investigate the effects of (+)-Catechin in female LDLr /  mice in vivo. (+)-Catechin lowered plasma cholesterol levels, reduced circulating T cell populations, and increased several beneficial short chain fatty acids in both the plasma and the faeces. It also decreased plaque size, lipid content, macrophage accumulation, and CD3⁺ T cell infiltration in the aortic root, while enhancing markers of plaque stability. RNA sequencing (RNA seq) of the thoracic aorta revealed modulation of key pathways involved in inflammatory signalling, hypertension and immune responses. Complementary studies in human aortic smooth muscle cells demonstrated that (+)-Catechin attenuated macropinocytosis and oxidised LDL uptake, processes linked to plaque progression, without promoting calcification. RNA seq identified several genes and pathways consistent with the compound’s anti atherogenic and plaque stabilising actions. Collectively, these findings provide new mechanistic insights into the beneficial cardiovascular effects of (+)-Catechin in female mice and support further evaluation of this flavanol in human clinical trials.

metadata.summary: Developing arteries must withstand pulsatile blood flow while remaining sufficiently flexible to accommodate changing hemodynamic demands. Endothelial interactions with perivascular cells and extracellular matrix are essential for this balance, but the signaling mechanisms that coordinate them remain incompletely understood. We previously showed that SH2 domain protein E (She), an endothelial adaptor protein implicated in ABL signaling, limits the size of the dorsal aorta (DA) in zebrafish embryos. Here, we investigated why zebrafish she mutants subsequently develop DA collapse and circulatory failure at 4–5 days post-fertilization. Before circulatory failure, the mutant DA retained an approximately circular cross-section and showed no detectable changes in the endothelial cell geometry, but exhibited increased distensibility during the cardiac cycle. Mutants had fewer perivascular stromal cells between the DA and posterior cardinal vein, smaller perivascular col1a1 and col5a1 expression domains, and reduced col1a1 transcript level. Single-cell RNA sequencing independently identified a reduced relative abundance of perivascular fibroblast subpopulation. In contrast, DA-associated mural cell numbers, laminin immunoreactivity, and local col4a1 transcript levels were not detectably altered. Ablation of pdgfrb-positive cells largely prevented DA narrowing and circulatory failure, while the nitric oxide donor sodium nitroprusside provided partial rescue. These findings support a contribution of mural cell-dependent vascular tone to collapse of the mechanically vulnerable DA. Mutants also exhibited cardiac chamber enlargement, increased atrial and bulbus arteriosus deformation, atrioventricular regurgitation, and increased Elastin B accumulation in the enlarged bulbus arteriosus. However, endocardial-specific She expression failed to rescue circulatory failure, supporting its requirement in vascular endothelium. Together, these findings link She function to perivascular fibroblast abundance, fibrillar collagen-gene expression, and arterial stability. They support a model in which impaired perivascular support renders the developing DA susceptible to mural cell-associated collapse, extending the role of She from early vessel-size regulation to maintenance of vascular function.

observations.title: SH2 Domain Protein E sustains perivascular fibroblasts to maintain arterial stability

observations.text: Myelin supports rapid and efficient neural communication and is implicated in brain development, learning, aging, and neurological disease. Although numerous magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) approaches have been proposed to characterize myelin in vivo, they have rarely been evaluated together within the same participants and across repeated acquisitions. To address these gaps, we introduce the Myelin Imaging Reliability and ReprOducibility Resource (MIRROR), an openly available multimodal test--retest MRI dataset of diffusion MRI (dMRI), inhomogeneous magnetization transfer imaging (ihMT), quantitative susceptibility mapping (QSM), MP2RAGE, T1w/T2w ratio mapping, and transverse relaxometry in 22 healthy adults. We evaluated gray--white matter differentiation, intermetric correspondence, test--retest reliability, and participant specificity across 27 myelin-sensitive metrics. Gray--white matter differentiation was strong for dMRI derivatives, MP2RAGE-derived R1, T1w/T2w, and ihMT, while being substantially weaker for QSM measures. Intermetric spatial correlations were generally strongest within acquisition or modeling families. Test--retest reliability was generally high, particularly for dMRI-derived metrics, but was more variable among QSM-, ihMT-, and R2*-derived measures. Regional spatial profiles were also highly participant-specific, with discriminability approaching its upper bound for most metrics. All imaging data, derived maps, and processing code are openly released. MIRROR provides a benchmark for characterizing the measurement properties and practical tradeoffs of scalable myelin-sensitive MRI methods, supporting principled acquisition selection and accelerating methodological development and validation.
